questions.question: What is the safest first principle when an older adult reports an unwitnessed fall?
choices: Assume it was mechanical if the patient is embarrassed
Reconstruct the event and evaluate injury, loss of consciousness, acute illness, medications, neurologic and cardiac causes before assigning a mechanism
Recommend bed rest without examination
Order every available test regardless of history
questions.explanation: An unwitnessed fall may represent syncope, seizure, trauma, toxicity, or environmental loss of balance; mechanism and disposition require a structured history and examination.

questions.question: An 81-year-old taking an anticoagulant strikes the head, has a memory gap, and develops worsening headache. What is the best disposition?
choices: Routine follow-up in one month
Home exercise only
Emergency head-injury evaluation
Stop anticoagulation permanently without assessment
questions.explanation: Anticoagulant exposure, amnesia, and worsening headache after head trauma raise concern for intracranial bleeding and require urgent emergency evaluation.

questions.question: Which orthostatic blood-pressure change supports orthostatic hypotension?
choices: A sustained drop of at least 20 mm Hg systolic or 10 mm Hg diastolic within three minutes of standing
A 5 mm Hg rise after exercise
Any single elevated seated pressure
A stable pressure with no symptoms
questions.explanation: This commonly used definition supports orthostatic hypotension, but symptoms, heart-rate response, baseline pressure, medications, and clinical context remain important.

questions.question: Which intervention has the strongest routine recommendation for community-dwelling adults age 65 or older who are at increased fall risk?
choices: Permanent activity restriction
Vitamin supplements alone
Sedating medication for fear
Exercise emphasizing gait, balance, functional and strength training
questions.explanation: The USPSTF recommends exercise interventions for increased-risk community-dwelling older adults; effective programs commonly train balance, gait, function, and strength.

questions.question: What is the best interpretation of a Timed Up and Go result?
choices: It definitively diagnoses the cause of every fall
It is one functional measure whose timing and movement quality should be interpreted with history, examination, device, pain, cognition, and baseline
A normal result guarantees no future fall
It should be forced even when the patient appears unsafe
questions.explanation: Functional tests help identify and track impairment but do not replace clinical reasoning or justify unsafe testing.

questions.question: Which fall history is most concerning for a cardiac cause?
choices: A clear trip on a loose rug with full recall
A stumble while carrying groceries
Sudden exertional loss of consciousness with a significant murmur and little warning
A slow controlled sit after knee pain
questions.explanation: Exertional syncope with structural-heart findings is a high-risk pattern that requires urgent cardiovascular evaluation rather than routine fall counseling.

questions.question: An older adult restricts all activity after a fall because of fear. What is the best response?
choices: Build a graded, appropriately supervised strength and balance plan while addressing specific hazards and confidence
Encourage permanent immobility
Remove all walking aids
Ignore the fear because it is psychological
questions.explanation: Fear-driven inactivity causes deconditioning and can increase future risk; graded training and individualized safety interventions support both confidence and function.

questions.question: Which is the best approach to a cane or walker?
choices: Any borrowed device is adequate
The patient should avoid it indoors
Device color determines effectiveness
Observe actual use and arrange appropriate selection, fit, maintenance, and training
questions.explanation: Incorrect device selection, height, technique, or maintenance can increase risk; physical or occupational therapy can optimize safe use.

questions.question: A patient has recurrent near-falls, short shuffling steps, reduced arm swing, and freezing during turns. What is the safest next step?
choices: Assume normal aging
Evaluate a progressive neurologic gait disorder, review medicines, protect mobility, and coordinate neurologic and therapy assessment
Prescribe bed rest
Treat only with a home night-light
questions.explanation: This is a parkinsonian gait pattern rather than normal aging and warrants diagnostic evaluation plus immediate mobility and fall-risk support.

questions.question: Why should bone health be addressed during fall prevention?
choices: Treating osteoporosis guarantees no falls
Bone health replaces gait training
Lower fracture susceptibility reduces injury severity even though it does not remove the causes of falling
Only patients with a prior hip fracture need assessment
questions.explanation: Fall and fracture prevention are complementary: mobility interventions reduce falls, while osteoporosis assessment and treatment can reduce the likelihood or severity of fragility injury.
